text: Wembley Stadium. The European Cup final. Extra time, and still nil–nil.
Barcelona have never won this trophy. They've been close twice — and both times it ended in heartbreak.
Then the referee gives a free-kick, about twenty-five metres from goal. And a Dutch centre-back with a famously powerful shot steps up to take it.
This is one free-kick, seen from ten different angles. By the end, you'll know why Barça fans still call it the most important goal in their history.
Angle one. The curse.
In nineteen sixty-one, Barça reached their first European Cup final, in Bern. They hit the woodwork again and again — the goalposts were square in those days — and lost three–two to Benfica.
In nineteen eighty-six, in Seville, they were overwhelming favourites against Steaua Bucharest. The game finished nil–nil. In the penalty shoot-out, Barça missed all four of their kicks.
So when they arrived at Wembley in nineteen ninety-two, the club carried thirty years of near-misses with it.
Angle two. The coach.
The man in charge was Johan Cruyff, four years into his time as coach. He had built a team that attacked, kept the ball, and took risks — the team people would call the Dream Team.
Before the final, according to his players, his team talk was famously short. Go out there and enjoy it.
It was Cruyff's way of taking away thirty years of pressure. Don't play against the curse. Play football.
Angle three. The orange shirts.
Barça didn't play the final in their famous blue and red. They played in their orange away kit.

For the team's Dutch players, orange had a special meaning: it's the colour of the Netherlands. And Ronald Koeman had already won a European Championship in orange — four years earlier, with his country, in nineteen eighty-eight.
That same year, he'd also won the European Cup with PSV Eindhoven. He knew exactly what nights like this felt like.
Angle four. The opponent.
Sampdoria were no pushovers. They had won the Italian league the year before — in an era when Italy's league was the strongest in the world.
Up front, they had Gianluca Vialli and Roberto Mancini — one of the most famous strike partnerships of the time.
And they had never won the European Cup either. Both clubs were chasing their first.
Angle five. Extra time.
The final was tense and close. Both sides had chances. Both goalkeepers made saves. After ninety minutes, it was still nil–nil.
For Barça fans, the thought was unavoidable: another final, another shoot-out, and memories of Seville.
Extra time began. Legs were tired. Everyone was waiting for one mistake.
Angle six. The foul.
In the hundred and eleventh minute, Barça's Eusebio was brought down just outside the Sampdoria area. Free-kick.
The position was central, around twenty-five metres out. Sampdoria lined up a wall. Several Barça players stood over the ball.
Everyone in the stadium knew who was most likely to shoot.
Angle seven. The touch.
It wasn't a straight shot. Hristo Stoichkov rolled the ball a short distance to the side.
José Mari Bakero stopped it dead, setting it up perfectly.
And that tiny movement changed the angle — moving the ball away from the wall's line of protection, and giving Koeman a clear view of the goal.
It was a routine. Not improvised. Practised.
Angle eight. The strike.
Koeman ran up and hit it with tremendous power, low and hard, past the wall and towards the far side of the goal.
The goalkeeper got nowhere near it. One–nil.
Koeman was a centre-back. But throughout his career, he scored an unusual number of goals for a defender — from free-kicks and penalties — because almost nobody struck the ball harder.
Angle nine. The steps.
There were still minutes to survive. Sampdoria pushed forward. Barça held on.
At the final whistle, the curse was gone.
At the old Wembley, the winners climbed the famous steps to the royal box to collect the trophy. The Barça captain, José Ramón Alexanko, lifted the European Cup — the first in the club's history.
Angle ten. What it started.
That night was the high point of Cruyff's Dream Team, which won four league titles in a row in the early nineties.
More importantly, it changed what Barça believed about themselves. They were no longer the club that always lost in Europe. They were champions.
In midfield that night was a twenty-one-year-old called Pep Guardiola, who would bring the club its next European Cups as coach.

And Koeman himself came back as Barça's coach in twenty twenty — during one of the hardest periods in the club's history. His time in charge was difficult. But at the club, he'll always be remembered for one thing first.
A centre-back from Groningen. One free-kick, in the hundred and twelfth minute.
Thirty years of heartbreak, ended in about half a second.
Which Barça moment should get the ten-angle treatment next? Tell me in the comments.
And for another goal that saved a whole season, watch the ten angles on Iniesta at Stamford Bridge.
